title: Four Ministers Pledge a Coordination Center in the Philippines. Balikatan Already Tested One
dek: During Balikatan 2026, Japanese and Australian personnel worked alongside American and Philippine forces at a coordination center in Camp Aguinaldo, according to the Philippines’ former military chief, whose account now offers a concrete point of comparison for the four governments’ October pledge and the institutional structure still awaiting definition.

body_paragraphs.text: When defense ministers from Australia, Japan, the Philippines and the United States pledged on Oct. 28 to establish a Combined Coordination Center (CCC) in the Philippines, their
joint statement published Nov. 10

introduced a new four-country undertaking with a name already familiar from the latest Balikatan exercise: during Balikatan 2026, forces from several nations had already worked inside a center at Camp Aguinaldo in Quezon City, where Gen. Romeo Brawner Jr., then the Philippines’ military chief,
said Japanese and Australian personnel took part

. That exercise experience gives the pledge a practical precedent, although the precise relationship between the Camp Aguinaldo facility and the proposed center, along with its eventual location, routine responsibilities and institutional identity, awaits an explanation from the governments involved.
Alongside the center pledge,
the statement also calls
for synchronized defense investments for the Philippines, expanded military exercises and closer policy consultations, yet the Australian release and Japan’s
Japanese-language version

describe the proposed center in terms that leave its location, opening date and staffing arrangements for subsequent decisions. When Manila Bulletin sought additional detail, the Philippine defense ministry offered a similarly limited account, while
Japan’s readout
of the Oct. 28 meeting and
Koizumi’s news conference
devoted greater attention to policy consultations, supply-and-services arrangements and negotiations on a military information-security agreement with Manila. Set against the ministers’
November 2025 readout
, the latest commitment to a four-country center is therefore the most conspicuous new institutional proposal in the published statements.
Long before the latest ministerial statement, the center’s name had appeared in accounts of U.S.–Philippine military exercises:
A U.S. military report

described a Combined Coordination Center synchronizing the two countries’ separate task forces during Balikatan 24 in 2024, and later that November, U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin and Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.
broke ground on a facility at Camp Aguinaldo
, headquarters of the Armed Forces of the Philippines, as they signed a bilateral General Security of Military Information Agreement (GSOMIA). Explaining the purpose of the facility,
the U.S. Defense Department said

it would support joint planning and coordinated responses to real-time incidents, including contingencies in the South China Sea, extending the center’s proposed role beyond the activities of a single military exercise.
During Balikatan 25,
U.S. military reporting

described a “secure, joint operations node” at which American and Philippine planners synchronized their respective task forces while each country retained authority within its own command structure, an arrangement that allowed the two militaries to coordinate their activities through a common planning venue. By Balikatan 2026, that structure had become part of a wider multinational exercise, with Adm. Samuel Paparo, then commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, saying that participants had “embedded this structure, including the newly inaugurated Combined Coordination Center,”
according to the command-sponsored Indo-Pacific Defense FORUM
. In that progression from bilateral planning to the participation of additional national forces lies the immediate operational background to the ministers’ subsequent proposal.
During the 2026 exercise, the Philippine Daily Inquirer reported
Brawner’s account
of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. observing a live-fire drill through the center alongside personnel from the Philippines, United States, Japan, Australia, France and Canada; in an
edited interview published by FORUM

in September, Brawner separately recalled “elements from Japan and Australia” working inside the facility. His remarks provide the clearest published description of those countries’ participation, although regular peacetime assignments and the specific information available to individual personnel remain matters for further clarification, particularly given that
U.S. Indo-Pacific Command said
the exercise’s common operating picture—a shared display of operational information—was available to eight nations.
When the joint statement reached the public in November, Philippine accounts portrayed a coordination mechanism at varying stages of development:
Manila Standard described
the center as a planned initiative on Nov. 12, whereas Defense Secretary Teodoro had told reporters a day earlier, “There will be a coordination mechanism. Right now, it is already operating,”
GMA News reported
. Teodoro indicated that the locations would be disclosed after agreement among the participating governments, and
the Philippine Daily Inquirer noted

that his remarks left the relationship to the earlier Balikatan facility open, suggesting that an exercise-era arrangement could already be functioning while the eventual four-country framework continued to take shape.
Looking beyond Camp Aguinaldo, USNI News described
U.S.-funded combined coordination centers

at several Philippine locations during Balikatan 2026, raising the possibility that the ministers’ proposal might draw on a network of existing exercise facilities, although the particular locations and their relationship to the new arrangement await identification. Alongside the center pledge, the four military chiefs also signed Terms of Reference for a Pacific Chiefs of Defense Cooperation Council,
cited in the joint statement
, which
Manila Bulletin says

address information sharing and cooperation on planning and logistics; the place of that council within the proposed CCC arrangements remains to be explained. In a related but geographically distinct proposal,
Brawner’s proposed communications links
to allied command centers in Japan and Australia would connect Philippine facilities with headquarters overseas.
Within the Camp Aguinaldo arrangement,
coordination allowed separate national task forces
to exchange plans and maintain a common operational picture while preserving their respective chains of command, a distinction worth carrying into any reading of
the October statement
and its pledge to create a coordination center. Although
Paparo has spoken
of future exercises directed “through coalition combined command centers,” the four ministers’ published commitment uses narrower institutional language; meanwhile,
Japan and the Philippines have an agreement
governing reciprocal military access, and
Koizumi also discussed

arrangements for exchanging supplies and services with partner forces. Those existing agreements facilitate the movement and support of military personnel, leaving the proposed center’s command relationships and decision-making authorities for its participating governments to establish.

As the governments consider how to turn exercise coordination into a standing arrangement, sharing classified information will depend on agreements negotiated between participating states: the U.S.–Philippine General Security of Military Information Agreement (GSOMIA) governs exchanges between Washington and Manila, while Japan and the Philippines were working toward a comparable agreement in October,
Koizumi said
. During Balikatan 2026,
a U.S.-provided common operating picture

relied on foreign-disclosure officers and data tagging to determine how information moved across national networks, demonstrating an exercise-specific procedure while leaving the access available to individual Japanese and Australian officers, and the rules of any eventual four-country classified-information framework, for participating governments to establish.
Once the troops and exercise staffs have dispersed, the center’s purpose becomes a question of routine activity and actual incidents, especially because the
2024 U.S. fact sheet
envisaged coordination during real-time contingencies as well as joint planning.
GMA News separately reported

that military-exercise coordination within the Armed Forces of the Philippines had moved from its Education and Training Command to Strategic Command, an organizational shift that offers some context for Manila’s account of an operating mechanism; nevertheless, the new
four-country statement
leaves peacetime billets, incident responsibilities and long-term financing to future arrangements. Although
USNI News identified
U.S. funding for facilities used during Balikatan, the financial arrangements for the proposed four-country initiative have yet to be publicly specified.

At Balikatan, Japanese and Australian personnel worked alongside their American and Philippine counterparts in a coordination center, according to the Philippines’ former military chief, establishing an exercise precedent for the multinational initiative now under discussion. Turning that experience into a standing arrangement would require the governments to determine which officers would serve there, what information each could receive and how the center would respond during maritime incidents, while the
ministers have pledged a CCC

whose ultimate foundation could be Camp Aguinaldo, a network of facilities or a distinct organization. The eventual choices on staffing, information access and routine responsibilities will establish how far the exercise-era arrangements develop into sustained four-country cooperation.

publisher_references.original_title: New mission network integrates allied, partner forces during Balikatan

verification.locator: May 15, 2026, by FORUM Staff. Classified official because FORUM is sponsored by USINDOPACOM and is not independent of the U.S. government (Laos Brief precedent for government-site sources), but it is a command-sponsored staff article, not an official command statement: the description of the center (at AFP headquarters, Camp Aguinaldo, a command and control hub between the AFP and USINDOPACOM for multinational coordination) is FORUM's. Adm. Samuel Paparo's words are direct quotes from the May 8, 2026 Balikatan closing ceremony in Manila and are attributed to him: 'The entire multinational force embedded this structure, including the newly inaugurated Combined Coordination Center'; future Balikatan exercises led from there '[Camp Aguinaldo]' (bracket is FORUM's) 'through coalition combined command centers'. Command naming: USINDOPACOM was restyled 'U.S. Pacific Command' as a secondary title from June 16, 2026 (pacom.mil release 'Department of War Restores U.S. Pacific Command Designation', seen in search excerpt); the Brief uses INDOPACOM for May 2026 events. Distinct from s18 (September 2026 FORUM interview).

publisher_references.original_title: PH, US, Japan, Australia establishing defense coordination center — Teodoro

verification.locator: Published Nov. 12, 2026 11:00 PHT. Ambush interview 'on Wednesday' (Nov. 11). Direct quote: 'There will be a coordination mechanism. Right now, it is already operating. And we may disclose certain locations upon agreement by the parties.' GMA paraphrase: interoperability requirements 'no longer limited to educational and training activities'. GMA's own statement, not a quote: exercise coordination 'previously handled by the AFP Education and Training Command, but has been transferred to Strategic Command'. Lede (GMA's words) places the center 'in Manila'.

publisher_references.original_title: Balikatan drills may expand beyond WPS, include more allies — Teodoro

verification.locator: Byline Gabryelle Dumalag, INQUIRER.net, 03:57 PM May 08, 2026 (article:published_time 2026-05-08T07:57Z). Balikatan 2026 closing ceremony and press briefing at Camp Aguinaldo. Section 'Triple C': 'the newly established Combined Coordination Center, also referred to as the "Triple C," inside Camp Aguinaldo'. Inquirer paraphrase, not quote: Paparo 'described the facility as a secure multinational command-and-control hub designed to coordinate multilateral operations and future Balikatan activities using encrypted communications networks shared among allies'; direct Paparo quote 'We've been working on this for five years. It's a reality.' Inquirer paraphrase of Brawner: Marcos 'monitored one of the recent live-fire drills in Ilocos through the center, alongside military personnel from the United States, Australia, France, Canada, Japan, and the Philippines'; goal 'to establish communication links with allied command centers outside the country, including those in Japan, Australia, and the US Indo-Pacific Command headquarters'. Squad chiefs to meet that afternoon on expanding Balikatan's area of operations via communications links, not troops abroad. Independent reporting of officials' statements; not evidence of standing billets. Retrieved 13 Nov 2026.

publisher_references.issuer: Indo-Pacific Defense Forum staff (USINDOPACOM-sponsored publication); interview with Gen. Romeo Brawner Jr.

verification.locator: Dated September 14, 2026, FORUM Staff; 'Correspondent Frances Mangosing contributed to this interview, which was edited to fit FORUM's format.' Brawner retired as AFP chief of staff in July 2026. Classified official on the s10 precedent (command-sponsored, not independent); the words are Brawner's, as edited by FORUM. Brawner: 'In the Balikatan 2026 exercise, we had not just the U.S. and the Philippines working together in a common command center, or Combined Coordinating Center, but we also had elements from Japan and Australia.' Stated plans, not facts: an AFP officer to be embedded in the U.S. Pacific Command ('We are just arranging the mechanics') and in Japan and Australia; 'we welcome these countries to be part of a command center, or control center, here in the Philippines.' The article uses 'U.S. Pacific Command' (post-June 2026 styling). Retrieved 13 Nov 2026.
